doc.title: Arturo Sandoval interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2023

title: Vibrato and singers
summary: He defends vibrato as expression and aid to intonation, and says the best thing an instrumentalist can do is copy a good singer.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: I had a question here that I wrote down and it was, was your vibrato influenced by hearing particular singers?

Absolutely. Some of them doing this: [audio interlude plays “When I Fall in Love” straight and with vibrato You see what I mean? They start like this, flat, and then toward the end of the note they start accelerating a little bit, the vibrato. It’s a different way. You know some of the classical players or some other people they’re very fond of another kind of playing. They don’t like to use vibrato at all. I’ve been criticized because of the vibrato. And I said man, vibrato is part of your expression. It’s part of the nuance of the saying within the note. You know also when you use a little vibrato you have a much better possibility to be in tune.

Because when you’re playing completely flat, you have to be very careful that you hit that note exactly in the center of the pitch. But this is the line of the pitch over here. When you do vibrato you’re doing this — and you have a good possibility to be around the center of the pitch you know. I don’t conceive a singer for example [sings without expression] When I fall in love.” I don’t get it. I don’t get it. It’s something missing there, internal expression and the best thing we could do as an instrumentalist is to copy a good singer.
Also can you imagine a string section not using vibrato what that would sound like.
The pitch is going to be horrible to start with. Yes. Yes.
